why: Follow the scheduler's rules exactly, but make each step fast: you repeatedly need the largest priority held by 2 or more live processes, and the two smallest indices at that priority. A max-heap of duplicated priorities and a min-heap of indices per priority do this in O(log n) per step.
hints: A naive scan per step is O(n) and there can be n steps. Which two lookups does each step need?
Each step needs (1) the largest priority with count >= 2 and (2) the two lowest indices with that priority. Then one process disappears and the other moves to priority p // 2.

Keep counts per priority, a min-heap of indices per priority, and a lazy max-heap of priorities whose count >= 2 (skip stale tops). Each step removes a process, so there are at most n-1 steps: O(n log n).
pitfalls: Priority 0 never triggers a step, even when shared.
The demoted process keeps its queue position; output survivors in original index order.
Demotion can create a new duplicate at p // 2 that may be larger than other pending ones, so push it back on the heap.
